title: Thousands of Nvidia B300s reportedly go up for sale after US chip rule
excerpt: GPU Mart says the US rule drove a surge of Nvidia B300 sales. A Shenzhen vendor told the Post he sells to Russians and Iranians too.
content_html:
Sellers are offering an unusually large number of Nvidia graphics processors, including thousands of B300s, after the US curbed Chinese firms’ remote access to AI chips. Three people told Kai Nicol-Schwarz of CNBC on Wednesday.

One of them, Jack Duhamel, is president of GPU Mart, a marketplace for AI infrastructure. He and another person said the surge in GPUs for sale came directly from the new rule. One seller told GPU Mart the rule was the reason for its sale, Duhamel said.

The chips were meant for data centres that rent computing power to Chinese companies, the two other people said.

From rule to resale

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced the remote access rule on 16 November. It took effect on 19 November.

On 17 November, Nvidia’s then interim CEO, Colette Kress, said the company was still studying the controls. She expected results to stay strong because demand far exceeds supply, CNBC reported.

Since then, sellers have floated deals for thousands of B300s, one of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, according to Duhamel and one of the people. Data centres in Asia are also trying to rent their spare capacity to US buyers, and rental prices have dipped. Nvidia has also reportedly stopped server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries.

Nvidia declined to comment to CNBC. The Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond.

“Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Shenzhen’s grey market

In China, the chips are still on offer. Joshua Yang found B300 servers for sale in Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei electronics market for The Washington Post. The Post could not verify that the chips were real.

The buyers are not only Chinese. Russians and Iranians have bought Nvidia chips at his stall for four or five years, hardware store owner Jason Cheng told the Post.

“We don’t care which country a customer comes from, as long as they can pay,” Cheng said.

China’s embassy in Washington told the Post that it opposes the US “abusing export control measures.”

Slow enforcement

A former official at the Bureau of Industry and Security told the Post that enforcement had stalled. The bureau’s head, Jeffrey Kessler, had to approve many routine actions himself, the former official said. The Commerce Department and the bureau did not respond to the Post.

Licensing data from the House Foreign Affairs Committee shows the administration approved nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, Reuters reported. Congress could add the Chip Security Act, which would require location checks for AI chips, to the defence bill it expects to pass next month.
